days.title: Homeostasis — Steady Internal Conditions
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define homeostasis.
  • Explain why organisms need stable internal conditions.
  • Identify examples of homeostasis in plants and animals.
  • Describe the roles of various organ systems in maintaining homeostasis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Homeostasis — maintenance of a stable internal environment.
  • Set point — the target value a system tries to maintain.
  • Sensor — detects changes.
  • Effector — produces the response.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Why Homeostasis Matters

Enzymes and cells work best under specific conditions (temperature, pH, ion concentrations). Without homeostasis, proteins denature and life processes fail.

B. Homeostatic Variables

VariableNormal Range
Body temperature (human)~36.5–37.5 °C
Blood pH~7.35–7.45
Blood glucose~70–110 mg/dL (fasting)
Osmotic balance~0.9% NaCl

C. Examples in Organisms

  • Animals: sweating, shivering, insulin/glucagon, kidney filtration
  • Plants: stomatal control, water uptake by roots, turgor regulation

💬 Let's Discuss

Your enzymes work best at about 37 °C and pH 7.4. Too hot and they denature; too acidic and they stop. Yet the world outside keeps changing: hot afternoons, cold mornings, salty meals, long hours without water. Homeostasis is the ability of an organism to keep its internal environment stable even when the external environment changes.

"Stable" does not mean fixed. Each variable has a set point and a normal range: body temperature about 36.5–37.5 °C, blood pH 7.35–7.45, fasting blood glucose about 70–110 mg/dL. Values move a little, and the body keeps pulling them back — like a driver making small steering corrections to stay in the lane.

Every homeostatic control has three parts. A sensor (receptor) detects a change, a control center (often the brain's hypothalamus or an endocrine gland) compares it with the set point and decides what to do, and an effector (a muscle or gland) makes the response. For example, when you overheat, temperature receptors signal the hypothalamus, which makes sweat glands (effectors) produce sweat.

Homeostasis covers many variables: thermoregulation (temperature), osmoregulation (water and salt balance, controlled mainly by the kidneys), and glucoregulation (blood sugar, controlled by insulin and glucagon). Plants have homeostasis too: they close stomata in drought to keep water.

Many diseases are failures of homeostasis: diabetes (glucose), heat stroke (temperature), dehydration (water balance). Common mistake: calling any life process homeostasis. Photosynthesis or reproduction are not about keeping a variable steady, so they are not homeostasis.

pairs.why: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions stable.
The set point is the target value the body tries to keep.
Sensors (receptors) detect changes from the set point.
Effectors are muscles or glands that carry out the response.
Normal human body temperature is about 36.5–37.5 °C.
Normal blood pH is about 7.35–7.45.
Normal fasting blood glucose is about 70–110 mg/dL.

scenarios.text: Body temperature rises during exercise.
scenarios.explanation: A rise in temperature is the change (stimulus) that sensors detect.

scenarios.text: Blood pH is normally 7.4.
scenarios.explanation: pH 7.4 is the target value — the set point.

scenarios.text: Sweat glands produce sweat.
scenarios.explanation: Sweat glands produce the response, so they are effectors.

scenarios.text: A plant closes stomata in drought.
scenarios.explanation: Closing stomata keeps water steady — plant homeostasis.

scenarios.text: Kidneys filter blood and adjust water.
scenarios.explanation: Kidneys balancing water and salt is osmoregulation.

scenarios.text: Insulin lowers blood glucose.
scenarios.explanation: Insulin returning glucose to normal is homeostasis.

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is keeping a stable internal environment.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an example of homeostasis?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis makes food; it does not keep a variable stable.

choices.label: To look more complex than others
To grow larger than their parents

questions.explanation: Stable conditions keep enzymes and cells working properly.

takeaways: Set points, sensors, and effectors maintain balance.
Enzymes work best under specific conditions.
Plants and animals both regulate homeostasis.

days.title: Negative Feedback Loops
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define negative feedback.
  • Identify components of a feedback loop.
  • Describe examples of negative feedback.
  • Explain how negative feedback maintains homeostasis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Negative feedback — response reverses the original stimulus.
  • Stimulus — change that triggers the loop.
  • Response — action that counteracts the stimulus.
  • Receptor, control center, effector — the three parts.

📚 Lesson Content

A. How Negative Feedback Works

  1. Stimulus — a change from the set point
  2. Receptor — detects the change
  3. Control center — processes the info
  4. Effector — produces a response
  5. Response — reverses the change

B. Examples

SystemStimulusResponse
ThermoregulationBody too hotSweating, vasodilation
ThermoregulationBody too coldShivering, vasoconstriction
Blood glucoseHigh glucoseInsulin released
Blood glucoseLow glucoseGlucagon released
OsmoregulationDehydrationADH released → water reabsorbed

💬 Let's Discuss

Most homeostasis works by negative feedback: the response opposes or reverses the change, bringing the variable back toward the set point. "Negative" does not mean bad; it means "opposite." A home air-conditioner is the classic model: when the room gets warmer than the set temperature, the thermostat turns the cooling on; when it gets cool enough, it turns it off.

Every loop has the same steps: stimulus (a change) → receptor (detects it) → control center (compares with the set point) → effector (acts) → response (reverses the change) → stimulus reduced, so the loop slows down.

Blood glucose: after you eat rice, glucose rises; the pancreas releases insulin, which makes cells take in glucose and the liver store it as glycogen, so glucose falls. Between meals glucose drops; the pancreas releases glucagon, which makes the liver release glucose. Two opposing hormones keep levels in range. Temperature: when hot, you sweat and blood vessels in the skin widen (vasodilation) to lose heat; when cold, you shiver and skin vessels narrow (vasoconstriction). Water: when dehydrated, the pituitary releases ADH, which makes kidneys reabsorb water, producing dark, concentrated urine. Calcium: low blood calcium triggers parathyroid hormone, which releases calcium from bone.

Negative feedback makes systems stable, which is why it is so common. Common mistake: thinking negative feedback stops the process forever. It simply reduces the response once the variable returns to normal, and starts again if the variable drifts away.

pairs.why: Negative feedback reverses the change and restores the set point.
The stimulus is the change away from the set point.
The receptor detects the change.
The control center compares the input with the set point and sends commands.
The effector produces the response.
The response counteracts the original change.

scenarios.text: Body temperature rises → sweating begins.
scenarios.explanation: Sweating lowers temperature, reversing the rise — negative feedback.

scenarios.text: Blood glucose is high → insulin released.
scenarios.explanation: Insulin lowers high glucose — negative feedback.

scenarios.text: Blood glucose is low → glucagon released.
scenarios.explanation: Glucagon raises low glucose — negative feedback.

scenarios.text: Body temperature drops → shivering.
scenarios.explanation: Shivering raises low temperature — negative feedback.

scenarios.text: A person is dehydrated → ADH released.
scenarios.explanation: ADH saves water when dehydrated — negative feedback.

scenarios.text: Blood calcium drops → PTH released.
scenarios.explanation: PTH raises low calcium — negative feedback.

questions.text: In negative feedback, the response does what to the stimulus?
Which hormone is released when blood glucose is HIGH?
questions.explanation: Insulin is released when blood glucose is high.

questions.text: Sweating when hot is an example of:
questions.explanation: Sweating cools the body, reversing the temperature rise.

takeaways: It consists of a stimulus, receptor, control center, effector, and response.
Most homeostatic mechanisms are negative feedback loops.

days.title: Positive Feedback Loops
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define positive feedback.
  • Differentiate positive from negative feedback.
  • Describe examples of positive feedback.
  • Explain why positive feedback must be short-lived.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Positive feedback — response amplifies the original stimulus.
  • Amplification — increases the stimulus.
  • Stop signal — external event that halts the loop.

📚 Lesson Content

A. How Positive Feedback Works

The response increases the original stimulus, causing further response. This cycle continues until an external event stops it.

B. Examples

SystemStimulusResponseStop
ChildbirthPressure on cervixOxytocin → more contractionsBaby delivered
Blood clottingVessel injuryPlatelets attract more plateletsClot formed
LactationSucklingProlactin → more milkStop nursing

C. Why It Must Stop

Runaway positive feedback is dangerous — e.g., uncontrolled clotting or runaway fever.

💬 Let's Discuss

Positive feedback is the opposite of negative feedback: the response increases or amplifies the original change, pushing the variable even further from where it started. Think of a microphone held too close to a speaker: the sound gets louder, is picked up again, gets louder still — until someone pulls the plug.

Because positive feedback runs away, it is rare in the body and used only for processes that must be finished quickly and then stopped. Each loop needs an end point — an outside event that breaks the cycle.

Childbirth: the baby's head presses on the cervix; stretch receptors signal the brain; the pituitary releases oxytocin; oxytocin makes the uterus contract harder, pushing the head down further, which causes more oxytocin. The loop ends when the baby is born and the pressure stops. (Doctors give synthetic oxytocin to start or speed labor.) Blood clotting: injured vessel walls activate platelets, which release chemicals that attract and activate more platelets, quickly forming a plug. The loop stops when the wound is sealed. Breastfeeding: the baby's sucking stimulates prolactin (milk production) and oxytocin (milk release); more sucking means more milk. It ends when the baby stops nursing.

When positive feedback happens where it should not, it can be dangerous: in very high fever, rising temperature speeds up metabolism, which makes even more heat; in severe blood loss, a weak heart pumps less blood, weakening itself further.

Common mistake: saying positive feedback is "good" and negative feedback is "bad." Negative feedback keeps us stable; positive feedback must be tightly limited.

pairs.why: Positive feedback amplifies the original change.
Amplification means the response makes the stimulus stronger.
In childbirth, oxytocin causes stronger contractions, which cause more oxytocin.
Activated platelets attract more platelets until a clot forms.
Nursing stimulates prolactin, and prolactin increases milk production.
An outside event, like birth or sealing a wound, stops the loop.

scenarios.text: Uterine contractions strengthen until baby is born.
scenarios.explanation: Contractions getting stronger until birth is positive feedback.

scenarios.text: Platelets release chemicals that attract more platelets.
scenarios.explanation: Platelets recruiting more platelets is positive feedback.

scenarios.text: Sweating to cool down.
scenarios.explanation: Sweating reverses rising temperature — negative feedback.

scenarios.text: Oxytocin release during labor.
scenarios.explanation: Oxytocin increasing contractions during labor is positive feedback.

scenarios.text: Insulin lowers blood sugar.
scenarios.explanation: Insulin reversing high glucose is negative feedback.

scenarios.text: Milk production increases with nursing.
scenarios.explanation: Nursing increasing milk output is positive feedback.

questions.text: In positive feedback, the response does what to the stimulus?
Which of the following is a positive feedback loop?
questions.explanation: Childbirth contractions build up by positive feedback; the others are negative feedback.

choices.label: It is too slow to help
It can run out of control

questions.explanation: Positive feedback must stop or it causes runaway, harmful effects.

takeaways: It must be stopped by an external event.
Runaway positive feedback can be dangerous.

days.title: Real-Life Homeostasis Examples
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Apply homeostasis concepts to real-life scenarios.
  • Describe plant homeostasis mechanisms.
  • Describe animal homeostasis mechanisms.
  • Analyze what happens when homeostasis fails.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Thermoregulation — temperature balance.
  • Osmoregulation — water/salt balance.
  • Glucoregulation — glucose balance.
  • Homeostatic failure — disease or death.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Animal Homeostasis

  • Temperature: sweating, shivering, vasodilation, vasoconstriction
  • Glucose: insulin, glucagon
  • Water: ADH, kidneys
  • pH: buffers, breathing rate

B. Plant Homeostasis

  • Water: stomatal opening/closing via guard cells
  • Temperature: transpiration cooling
  • Nutrients: root uptake, vascular transport
  • Turgor: vacuole regulation

C. When Homeostasis Fails

FailureResult
Thermoregulation fails (high)Heat stroke
Thermoregulation fails (low)Hypothermia
Glucose regulation failsDiabetes
Osmoregulation failsDehydration or edema

💬 Let's Discuss

Homeostasis is easiest to understand through situations you actually experience in the Philippines.

A hot afternoon in PE class. Muscles release heat; the hypothalamus detects rising blood temperature and triggers sweating and vasodilation (skin looks flushed). Evaporating sweat carries heat away. On humid days sweat evaporates slowly, so cooling is weaker — that is why heat index matters. If water is not replaced, sweating stops and temperature climbs above 40 °C: heat stroke, a failure of thermoregulation and a medical emergency.

A cold night in Baguio. Temperature falls; you shiver (muscle activity makes heat), and skin vessels constrict to keep warm blood near the core. If heat loss wins, body temperature drops below 35 °C — hypothermia.

A big lunch. Blood sugar rises, insulin is released, and glucose is stored. In diabetes mellitus, the pancreas makes too little insulin (type 1) or cells ignore it (type 2), so glucose stays high and damages vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys.

A day without drinking water. Blood becomes more concentrated; ADH is released; kidneys save water, so urine becomes small in amount and dark yellow. You also feel thirsty — a behavioral response.

Plants in summer. When water loss through leaves exceeds uptake by roots, cells lose turgor and the plant wilts. Guard cells close stomata to reduce water loss.

Common mistake: thinking dehydration and heat stroke are the same. Dehydration can lead to heat stroke, but heat stroke is the failure of temperature control itself.

pairs.why: Thermoregulation keeps body temperature in range.
Osmoregulation balances water and salts.
Glucoregulation keeps blood glucose in range.
Heat stroke is thermoregulation failing on the hot side.
Hypothermia is body temperature falling too low.
Diabetes is a failure of blood glucose regulation.

scenarios.text: A person exercises in hot weather.
scenarios.explanation: In heat, the body sweats and widens skin blood vessels.

scenarios.text: A person walks in the cold.
scenarios.explanation: In cold, the body shivers and narrows skin blood vessels.

scenarios.text: A plant wilts.
scenarios.explanation: A plant wilts when it loses more water than it takes in.

scenarios.text: A person eats a large meal.
scenarios.explanation: After a large meal, insulin is released.

scenarios.text: A person hasn't drunk water all day.
scenarios.explanation: Dehydration triggers ADH, which concentrates urine.

scenarios.text: A marathon runner collapses with heat stroke.
scenarios.explanation: Collapse from heat stroke means thermoregulation failed.

questions.text: Which is a plant homeostatic mechanism?
questions.explanation: Opening and closing stomata is a plant homeostatic mechanism.

questions.text: What happens when thermoregulation fails in hot weather?
questions.explanation: Failure of thermoregulation in heat causes heat stroke.
ADH regulates water balance through the kidneys.

takeaways: Homeostasis maintains temperature, water, glucose, and pH.
Plants regulate water via stomata; animals via kidneys and hormones.
Real-life examples: sweating, shivering, insulin, ADH.
